**The impact of social media use on body image and disordered eating behaviors: Content matters more than duration of exposure** (URL: [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10363994/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10363994/)) 

*(Published Apr 2023\)*

* Based on research, authors conclude that “**interventions targeting negative consequences of social media use should focus on addressing content consumed**, rather than time spent on social media platforms”  
* Researchers surveyed “two demographically diverse undergraduate samples” in 2015 and then 2022, analyzing the relation of various social media uses and disordered body image/eating behavior. The study thus both compared the results of the two samples with one another (especially due to the pandemic’s impact on use in 2022), and more importantly for our research was the first to examine whether associations between SMU and body image are impacted by specific types of content consumed  
* Participants were undergrad students “at a large University in the northeastern United States.” and the methodology was two online self-report surveys (one in 2015 and one in 2022\) on SMU and body-image/eating behaviors  
  * For SMU, participants indicated the types and total amount of accounts they used, and self-reported estimate of minutes spent each day  
  * For body image, three questionnaires were used to evaluate behaviors/self-perception: the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), Fear of Negative Appearance Evaluation Scale (FNAES), and Eating Disorder Examination — Questionnaire  
  * Participants’ mean age was just above 19 y.o. in both years’ samples  
      
* Participants who were exposed to weight loss content or body positivity/neutrality content on social media reported “significantly higher BMI, lower body appreciation, greater fears of negative appearance evaluation, and more frequent binge eating, and laxative use” than those who were not  
  * Shows that specific types of content on social media play a major role in impact on body image. Supports idea that social media should be used intentionally to avoid potential negative effects  
* **Amount of SMU** each day **was** “**significantly and inversely associated with BAS scores and significantly and positively correlated with BMI, ratings on the FNAES, and frequency of binge eating and vomiting**”  
  * Breaking this down, it was **specifically exposure to weight-loss content on SM** which **affected BAS and FNAES scores and frequency of binge eating** rather than just time spent on SM overall.  
  * Similarly, “**respondents spending more time on SM** … **only reported high binge frequency if they were also exposed to weight loss content**”   
  * Therefore, while SMU is clearly associated with negative body image effects, it is also the weight loss content presented to users/seeked out by users on SM which is responsible for this association–not the SM itself  
    ![][image1]  
* Interestingly, the analysis found that consuming **body-positivity or neutral content** on social media **did not benefit or harm participants’ body image perception and eating disorder behaviors**  
  * Note one limitation that the survey grouped body positivity and neutrality as one, while they may vary significantly in impact (perhaps body positivity could have a positive impact and content self-reported as “neutral” negative ones, for instance)  
* Over time, note the observation that “**participants in** the **2022** sample **endorsed significantly more body image disturbances and disordered eating behaviors compared to** those in the **2015** sample,” and also “**participants in** the **2022** sample **reported** a **greater** amount of **time spent on SM and accounts held**”   
  * Shows that this subject is very much a growing issue, and the authors argue this is perhaps a function of the COVID pandemic and post-pandemic periods. Would be interesting to see the comparison now after a few more years have passed  
* The overall conclusion of the study is that “**time spent on SM and number of platforms accessed were generally unrelated to outcomes of interest**,” but “**there were significant** main **effects of viewing weight loss content on SM on** indices of **body image satisfaction and disordered eating behaviors**, with exposure to weight loss content associated with lower body appreciation, greater fears of negative appearance evaluation, and more frequent binge eating”
